opening_message:
Ticket 1: Christopher Myers (employee ID E012) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E012.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Employee is a full-time Analyst requesting write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write (admin only if their role owns the system; Analyst does not own Source Code). Requested level is write, which is within policy, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E012 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note said full-time, but security records govern here). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.
reason: E012 (Christopher Myers) requested write access to Source Code. There is conflicting evidence: the HR note lists employment type as full_time and recommends write, while the Security note says the Security DB records E012 as a contractor with basic security training, which governs access decisions. Under policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training (never admin). Since E012 has only basic training, the maximum allowable level is read. The requested write exceeds the maximum, so the maximum (read) is granted.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E012 (Christopher Myers) requests write access to Source Code.

Two notes from team memory:

Note 1 (likely HR): role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommendation write. Comment says full-time may have up to write; Analyst does not own Source Code, so admin not allowed; requested write is within policy, recommend write.

Note 2 (likely Security): role Analyst, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read. Comment says security DB shows contractor with basic training; contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

So there is conflict: HR says full-time → write allowed. Security says contractor with basic training → read max.

The security note says "security records govern here" and says the HR note said full-time but security says contractor. Hmm. As the Approver, I need to decide. Which source prevails?

The policy: contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. Full-time: up to write, admin only if role owns system.

The two agents disagree on employment type. The Security agent looked up in own database and says contractor with basic training. HR says full_time. The Security note explicitly says security records govern.

I need to make a final decision. Given conflicting evidence, I should apply the more restrictive/secure option? Typically in these scenarios, the security record governs access. Also the employee facts: we have two conflicting notes on employment type. The recommended access from Security is read, from HR is write.

Given the ambiguity, the safe decision is the more restrictive: read. The security record indicates contractor with basic training, which maxes at read. The requested level is write, which is above max, so grant read.

Actually, let me consider: the note says "Security DB shows E012 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note said full-time, but security records govern here)." The security agent claims security records govern. As Approver, I might decide based on security records. Grant read.

I'll submit read.
